term_glossary.tooltip: Layers of Cryptographic Keys: an OCP architecture for hardware-rooted storage key protection and lifecycle control.
Self-encrypting drive: a storage device that encrypts media data internally.
Key Management Block: the protected Caliptra component allowed to execute L.O.C.K. operations, read MEKs, and program the encryption engine.
Media Encryption Key: up to 512 bits of key material used by a storage encryption-engine slot to protect media data.
Rendering encrypted data irrecoverable by securely eliminating the key material required to decrypt it.
Device Protection Key: a device-unique root key derived from hardware secrets.
Management Protection Key: an ordered, optional layer used to represent an administrative boundary.
Epoch Protection Key: the active epoch layer formed from a hardware epoch key and software epoch key.
Hardware Epoch Key: one of 4 to 16 256-bit values provisioned in fuse slots.
Software Epoch Key: durable software-controlled epoch material combined with the HEK.
Volatile Encryption Key: a lazily generated key that protects enabled MPKs held in volatile memory.
MEK Derivation Key: a device-unique key used in random-key inner wrapping and derived-MEK generation.
Hybrid Public Key Encryption: the public-key envelope used to establish protected access material.
Special Function Register: a memory-mapped register used for protected MEK transfer and control.
A metadata field identifying the target storage encryption engine.
A metadata field identifying a key slot within the target encryption engine.
Known-answer test: an optional command used to verify MEK transfer behavior against a known result.
The hardware root-of-trust environment hosting the KMB; L.O.C.K. v1.1 targets version 2.1 or newer.

slides.title: Retiring Data Should Not Require Retiring the Drive
slides.subtitle: L.O.C.K. makes the key lifecycle an explicit hardware security boundary.

bullets.text: Organizations may physically destroy usable drives because proving data destruction is difficult.
Cryptographic erase can retire protected data by eliminating the required key material.
A drive can move to another tenant or environment without carrying the prior epoch’s decrypt capability.
L.O.C.K. defines interoperable security behavior for self-encrypting storage controllers.

figure.alt: Animation contrasting physical drive destruction with cryptographic retirement and safe drive reuse.
figure.caption: A key-lifecycle boundary can preserve the hardware while retiring the protected data.

slides.title: Assume Powerful Attackers—But Separate Security from Availability
slides.subtitle: The guarantees remain meaningful even when ordinary controller software is compromised.

bullets.text: Attackers may control firmware, observe or modify external traffic, or gain physical access to non-protected storage.
Device-unique secrets, the KMB, and the engine key path remain inside the hardware-rooted boundary.
Compromise outside that boundary must not reveal usable MEKs or revive erased key state.
Denial of service, media damage, or refusal to process I/O are not confidentiality failures.

figure.alt: Threat model matrix separating attacker capabilities, protected assets, and availability exclusions.
figure.caption: The model protects key confidentiality and erasure semantics, not uninterrupted service.

slides.title: Three Guarantees Turn Key Handling into an Architecture
slides.subtitle: Each guarantee constrains both storage and controller implementation.

bullets.text: MEK material must not become readable by ordinary firmware, host software, or external interfaces.
Encrypted media remains unintelligible without the intended hierarchy and active epoch.
Destroyed epoch or parent-key state cannot be reconstructed from residual device information.
Only the KMB may read an MEK and program the storage encryption engine.

figure.alt: Three-part diagram showing key secrecy, data protection, and irreversible key-state retirement.
figure.caption: The protected path connects confidentiality, correct use, and irreversible retirement.

slides.title: Policy Can Cross Firmware; Plaintext MEKs Cannot
slides.subtitle: The KMB is the narrow bridge between lifecycle commands and the encryption engine.

bullets.text: A host or key service requests lifecycle actions through controller APIs.
Ordinary firmware can carry commands and wrapped objects without seeing plaintext MEKs.
Caliptra’s KMB unwraps, derives, loads, zeroizes, and reports key state inside the root of trust.
MEKs move through dedicated secure registers from the KMB to the encryption engine.

figure.alt: Animation showing control messages passing through firmware while MEK material remains inside the KMB-to-encryption-engine protected path.
figure.caption: Commands are observable; plaintext MEK transfer remains inside the protected boundary.

slides.title: L.O.C.K. Complements Storage Protocols and Security Frameworks
slides.subtitle: It standardizes internal key protection without forcing a single host protocol.

bullets.text: The architecture is not limited to NVMe and can be integrated into different storage-controller command sets.
It can support TCG Opal, Enterprise, and Key Per I/O management models.
Version 1.1 targets the Caliptra Subsystem 2.1 or newer KMB security services.
The design can align with OCP S.A.F.E.™ while keeping each framework’s scope distinct.

figure.alt: Layer diagram showing L.O.C.K. between host security protocols, Caliptra, and OCP S.A.F.E.™ using their official logos.
figure.caption: L.O.C.K. defines the controller’s key boundary, not a replacement for every surrounding protocol.

slides.title: Trust the Narrow Path, Not the Whole Controller
items: Cryptographic retirement can separate data destruction from drive destruction.
The threat model allows compromised ordinary firmware without surrendering plaintext MEKs.
The KMB is the only component permitted to read MEKs and program the encryption engine.
Availability failures are distinct from confidentiality and irreversible-erasure guarantees.
L.O.C.K. complements existing storage protocols and OCP security frameworks.

slides.title: Check the L.O.C.K. Trust Model
slides.subtitle: Answer both questions once to continue. Correctness is not required, and you can retry.

questions.prompt: Which component is allowed to read a plaintext MEK and program the storage encryption engine?

choices.text: The Caliptra Key Management Block
Ordinary drive firmware
choices.feedback_incorrect: Firmware may carry commands and wrapped objects, but plaintext MEKs remain inside the protected KMB path.

choices.text: The host operating system
choices.feedback_incorrect: The host requests lifecycle actions; it does not receive plaintext MEKs from the device.

choices.text: The flash translation layer
choices.feedback_incorrect: Media-management logic is outside the protected MEK-reading boundary.

questions.feedback_correct: Correct. The KMB is the only entity permitted to read MEKs and program the engine.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Follow the protected path: KMB to secure registers to encryption engine.

questions.prompt: Which conditions fit the L.O.C.K. threat model? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Ordinary controller firmware may be compromised
External traffic may be observed or modified
Protected device-unique secrets remain inside their hardware boundary
The architecture guarantees uninterrupted service
Physical media damage must always be recoverable

questions.feedback_correct: Correct. L.O.C.K. protects key confidentiality and lifecycle semantics under strong attacker capabilities; it does not guarantee availability.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Separate confidentiality and irreversible erasure from availability or physical media survival.

modules.title: Key Hierarchy and Lifecycle
modules.subtitle: Four layers, three persistence classes, and two MEK strategies.

slides.title: OCP L.O.C.K.
slides.subtitle: Key Hierarchy and Lifecycle

slides.title: Follow Every Layer Through Its Lifecycle
slides.subtitle: By the end of this course, you will be able to:
objectives: Build the protection hierarchy from the device root to an engine-ready MEK.
Distinguish fuse, durable-flash, and volatile key state.
Explain MPK and epoch transitions, including their reset behavior.
Compare double-wrapped random MEKs with derived MEKs.

slides.title: Each Layer Adds a Different Administrative Boundary
slides.subtitle: The final MEK secret is the ordered result of device, management, and epoch protection.

bullets.text: A DPK binds the hierarchy to a specific storage controller.
Zero or more ordered MPKs represent customer, fleet, or organizational boundaries.
An EPK combines hardware and software epoch material for the current environment.
The resulting MEK secret protects random or derived MEKs; an MDK secures the final device-local path.

figure.alt: Animation building the DPK, ordered MPKs, EPK, MEK secret, MDK, and engine key path layer by layer.
figure.caption: The hierarchy is ordered: changing any active parent changes access to the protected MEK state.

slides.title: Persistence Determines What a Reset Can—and Cannot—Change
slides.subtitle: Fuses establish roots, flash retains policy state, and volatile memory holds enabled working state.

bullets.text: Device secrets and 4 to 16 HEK slots survive resets and establish immutable hardware roots.
Locked MPKs, SEK state, counters, and wrapped objects persist in flash.
Enabled MPKs, VEK-protected working material, HPKE private state, and loaded MEKs live in protected runtime memory.
The KMB recreates device-local roots, establishes fresh HPKE state, and lazily creates a VEK when needed.

figure.alt: Matrix mapping fuse, durable flash, and volatile state to cold-reset behavior.
figure.caption: A reset policy is meaningful only when each key’s persistence class is explicit.

slides.title: An MPK Moves from Locked Storage to Enabled Runtime State
slides.subtitle: HPKE grants access; the VEK protects the working copy.

bullets.text: An MPK can persist as a protected durable object without being usable for MEK operations.
Authorized HPKE material lets the KMB validate and recover the management layer.
The KMB keeps the active MPK inside protected volatile memory under the VEK.
Cold reset removes enabled working state; durable locked state can be enabled again after fresh authorization.

figure.alt: Animation showing a locked MPK being authorized through HPKE and protected by the VEK in enabled volatile state.
figure.caption: Locked is durable; Enabled is a protected runtime condition.

slides.title: Soft and Hard Epoch Changes Solve Different Operational Problems
slides.subtitle: Choose the transition according to whether the drive stays inside the trusted environment.

bullets.text: The active epoch combines a selected HEK fuse slot with durable SEK state.
Rotate the software-controlled epoch for an operational or tenant boundary while the hardware remains trusted.
Move to a different hardware epoch root before a drive leaves the environment or crosses a stronger ownership boundary.
Retiring an epoch removes the parent material needed to recover MEKs protected under that epoch.

figure.alt: Animation contrasting soft software-epoch rotation with a hard hardware-epoch transition.
figure.caption: A soft boundary rotates SEK state; a hard boundary moves to a different HEK root.

slides.title: Random and Derived MEKs Reach the Same Protected Engine Boundary
slides.subtitle: Their creation and recovery paths differ, but plaintext key material stays inside the KMB.

bullets.text: A generated MEK is inner-wrapped with the MDK using AES-ECB, then outer-protected with the MEK secret using preconditioned AES-GCM.
A CMAC KDF combines an input seed with the MDK path to recreate key material when needed.
The random-key outer envelope authenticates its protected object; derived keys may include a 128-bit checksum.
Random keys preserve wrapped objects; derived keys trade storage for deterministic regeneration.

figure.alt: Split-path diagram comparing double-wrapped random MEKs with CMAC-KDF-derived MEKs.
figure.caption: Both paths terminate inside the KMB-to-engine protected transfer boundary.

slides.title: Every Layer Has a Purpose, Location, and Retirement Rule
items: The ordered hierarchy is DPK, zero or more MPKs, and an EPK before the MEK secret protects MEK state.
HEKs live in 4 to 16 fuse slots; SEK state supplies the software-controlled half of an epoch.
Locked MPKs persist, while Enabled MPKs are VEK-protected volatile working state.
Soft and hard epoch transitions represent different operational boundaries.
Random MEKs are double wrapped; derived MEKs are recreated through the device-local KDF path.

slides.title: Check the Key Hierarchy
slides.subtitle: Answer both questions once to continue. Correctness is not required, and you can retry.

questions.prompt: Which two components form the active Epoch Protection Key?

choices.text: HEK and SEK
DPK and VEK
choices.feedback_incorrect: The DPK is the device root and the VEK protects volatile working state; neither pair defines the active epoch.

choices.text: MPK and MDK
choices.feedback_incorrect: MPKs are optional management layers, while the MDK secures the device-local MEK path.

choices.text: HPKE public and private keys
choices.feedback_incorrect: HPKE establishes protected access material but does not define the epoch.

questions.feedback_correct: Correct. A selected Hardware Epoch Key and Software Epoch Key form the EPK.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The epoch combines a hardware-rooted HEK with software-controlled SEK state.

questions.prompt: Which lifecycle statements are accurate? Select all that apply.

choices.text: A Locked MPK may persist in durable protected storage
An Enabled MPK is protected in volatile KMB state
Cold reset clears enabled working state
A derived MEK must always be stored as a wrapped key object
A soft epoch transition always consumes a new HEK fuse slot

questions.feedback_correct: Correct. Durable locked state and volatile enabled state serve different parts of the lifecycle.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Derived keys can be regenerated, and a soft transition changes software epoch state without necessarily moving to another HEK slot.

slides.thank_you_message: You have completed Module 2: Key Hierarchy and Lifecycle.

modules.title: Controller Integration and Compliance
modules.subtitle: Translate the security model into interfaces, state machines, and mandatory behavior.

slides.title: OCP L.O.C.K.
slides.subtitle: Controller Integration and Compliance

slides.title: Turn the Model into a Controller Contract
slides.subtitle: By the end of this course, you will be able to:
objectives: Separate the control mailbox from the protected MEK-transfer interface.
Read the MEK SFR layout and cache identity fields.
Sequence initialization, mixing, generation, load, derivation, and zeroization.
Map resets and the 13 mandatory behaviors to an integration checklist.

slides.title: Commands and Key Transfer Use Different Interfaces
slides.subtitle: The separation keeps policy traffic flexible while constraining plaintext MEK movement.

bullets.text: A mailbox carries L.O.C.K. requests, identifiers, wrapped objects, status, and reports.
Dedicated SFRs carry up to 512 bits of MEK material, metadata, auxiliary data, and control.
Both paths terminate in the KMB, but ordinary firmware cannot read plaintext key transfer.
ENGINE_ID and SLOT_ID bind an operation to the intended encryption-engine location.

figure.alt: Animation showing mailbox traffic terminating at the Caliptra KMB and a separate protected SFR transfer carrying plaintext MEK material from the KMB to an explicitly selected encryption-engine slot.
figure.caption: Control is message-oriented; plaintext MEK transfer is register-bound and protected.

slides.title: The SFR Map Makes Key Transfer Explicit and Auditable
slides.subtitle: A compact register window couples key bytes, identity, optional data, and one command.

bullets.text: 64 bytes at the base address carry up to 512 bits of key material.
20 bytes at base plus 0x40 identify engine, slot, key length, and cache context.
32 bytes at base plus 0x60 carry command-specific auxiliary data.
The register at base plus 0x80 selects Load, Unload, Zeroize, or optional KAT behavior.

figure.alt: Register map showing the 64-byte MEK, 20-byte metadata, 32-byte AUX, and CTRL regions plus engine and slot identity.
figure.caption: The SFR contract binds a key operation to explicit engine, slot, length, and control fields.

slides.title: Every MEK Operation Begins with an Explicit Secret Context
slides.subtitle: Initialization and ordered mixing precede generation, load, or derivation.

bullets.text: INITIALIZE_MEK_SECRET starts a fresh operation context from the active hierarchy.
Zero or more MIX_MEK_SECRET operations add ordered context before a final key action.
Generate or load a random MEK object, or derive a MEK from supplied seed material.
The KMB loads the selected engine slot; unload and zeroize commands remove usable runtime state.

figure.alt: Animation showing initialization, optional ordered MPK mixing, and exactly one final action: generate a wrapped random key, load a random key into an engine slot, or derive and load a key into an engine slot.
figure.caption: The state machine prevents a final MEK action from occurring outside an initialized hierarchy context.

slides.title: Map Product APIs to Five L.O.C.K. Operation Families
slides.subtitle: The host-facing command set may vary, but the security semantics must remain visible.

bullets.text: Report capabilities, supported algorithms, HEK metadata, limits, and current state.
Provision or authorize management layers and construct the active MEK-secret context.
Generate, import, derive, load, unload, and zeroize MEKs for explicit engine slots.
Rotate epochs, handle reset boundaries, report measurements, and expose compliance-relevant evidence.

figure.alt: Five grouped host API families for discovery, management layers, MEK operations, epoch transitions, and evidence.
figure.caption: A product can choose its transport while preserving the L.O.C.K. operation semantics.

slides.title: Reset Semantics Are Part of the Security Contract
slides.subtitle: Conformance requires both correct cryptography and correct state transitions.

bullets.text: Derive HEK and MDK state, create fresh HPKE state, and generate a VEK lazily when volatile MPK protection is first needed.
Preserve HEK, MDK, and VEK state while regenerating HPKE state.
Preserve the same device-local and volatile protection roots while rotating HPKE access state.
Table 56 defines 13 required behaviors covering hardware roots, reporting order, protected transfer, algorithms, lifecycle, and zeroization.

figure.alt: Matrix comparing cold reset, warm reset, firmware update, and the mandatory compliance baseline.
figure.caption: A compliant implementation must preserve or recreate each key class exactly as the reset model specifies.

slides.title: Integrate the Boundary, Not Just the Algorithms
items: Mailbox commands and protected MEK-transfer SFRs are separate interfaces with different exposure rules.
The 64-byte MEK, 20-byte metadata, 32-byte AUX, and CTRL regions make engine programming explicit.
Initialize and optional ordered mixing occur before random-key or derived-key final actions.
Host transports may differ, but capability, lifecycle, key, epoch, and evidence semantics must remain intact.
Cold reset, warm reset, firmware update, and the 13 mandatory requirements are all part of conformance.

slides.title: Check the Integration Contract
slides.subtitle: Answer both questions once to continue. Correctness is not required, and you can retry.

questions.prompt: What must begin a new MEK-secret operation context?

choices.text: INITIALIZE_MEK_SECRET
LOAD_MEK
choices.feedback_incorrect: Loading is a final key action and requires an initialized context first.

choices.text: REPORT_HEK_METADATA
choices.feedback_incorrect: HEK reporting is a boot-time disclosure requirement, not a MEK-secret initializer.

choices.text: KAT
choices.feedback_incorrect: KAT is an optional register-path test, not the hierarchy-context initializer.

questions.feedback_correct: Correct. INITIALIZE_MEK_SECRET creates the context before optional MIX operations and a final MEK action.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The required order begins with initialization, may include ordered mixing, and ends with one final MEK operation.

questions.prompt: Which statements belong to a compliant integration? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Plaintext MEKs transfer through the protected SFR path
ENGINE_ID and SLOT_ID bind an operation to a target
Warm reset and firmware update regenerate HPKE state
Ordinary firmware may read the MEK region for diagnostics
The host transport must always be NVMe

questions.feedback_correct: Correct. The protected transfer, explicit target identity, and reset-time HPKE rotation are core integration behaviors.
questions.feedback_incorrect: L.O.C.K. is transport-independent, and ordinary firmware must not gain plaintext MEK access.
